newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow mayor Luzhkov says Ukraine city is Russia's.
newsitem.headline: Moscow mayor Luzhkov says Ukraine city is Russia's.

text.p: Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, one of his country's most powerful politicians, called publicly on Thursday for Russia to lay claim to the Ukrainian city of Sevastopol, main base of the disputed Black Sea Fleet.

Luzhkov, evidently courting nationalist opinion in Russia, argued in Izvestia newspaper that Ukraine had no legal title to the city because of Sevastopol's history as a separate entity from the rest of the Crimean peninsula.

The city's population is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking but it has been governed from Kiev since Ukrainian independence in 1991. Russia and Ukraine, after five years of wrangling, are close to an agreement under which Russia will lease most of the naval base for its Black Sea ships, thus implicitly recognising Ukrainian sovereignty.
This in turn will clear the way for signing of a much-delayed bilateral treaty between the two largest post-Soviet states.
Luzhkov said Russia's current negotiating position was out of line with international law and historical reality.
"In negotiations with Ukraine the Russian side should raise the question not of leasing Sevastopol but of observing all existing legal acts," Luzhkov wrote.

"In the text of the treaty between Russia and Ukraine it is essential to confirm the Russian status of the city of Sevastopol -- part of the Russian Federation -- as the main naval base of the Russian Black Sea Fleet."

Luzhkov, re-elected with a big majority this year and hugely popular in the Russian capital, is often mentioned as a possible successor to President Boris Yeltsin. His article appeared likely to cause anger in Kiev.
He described Sevastopol as a city "literally drenched in the blood of Russians", a reference to its fate as a battleground both in the 19th century Crimean War and in World War Two.

Russia conquered the Crimean peninsula in the 1780s and built the Sevastopol naval base almost immediately. Crimea was transferred to Ukraine from Russia in 1954 but Russian nationalists argue this did not affect Sevastopol's special status.
